title: Event Sourcing & CQRS
description: Learn event sourcing — storing events instead of state — and CQRS, the pattern that separates read and write models for optimal performance.

segments.text: Most systems store current state. Your bank balance is 500 dollars, period. But what if instead of storing the balance, you stored every transaction that led to it? Deposit 1000, withdraw 300, deposit 200, withdraw 400. That's event sourcing.

In event sourcing, the event log is the source of truth, not the current state. Events are facts — they describe things that happened and are immutable. You never update or delete an event. To fix a mistake, you append a compensating event.

To get the current state, you replay all events from the beginning. Event one: account created. Event two: deposited 1000. Event three: withdrew 300. After replaying, your balance is 700. The state is derived, not stored directly.
segments.thought_prompt: Replaying millions of events sounds slow. How would you optimize this?

segments.text: You optimize with snapshots. Periodically save the current state as a checkpoint. To rebuild, load the latest snapshot and only replay events that came after it. This gives you the benefits of event sourcing without replaying the entire history every time.

Event sourcing gives you a complete audit trail for free. You can debug by replaying events. You can build new features by reprocessing old events. You can answer questions about history that you never anticipated needing. It's incredibly powerful.

But here's the challenge. Your write model is optimized for appending events. Your read model needs fast queries — show me all orders over 100 dollars from last month. These are fundamentally different access patterns. One model can't serve both well.

CQRS, Command Query Responsibility Segregation, splits your system into two sides. The command side handles writes and appends events. The query side maintains optimized read models built by projecting events. Different data stores for different purposes.

Projections are the bridge. They consume events and update read-optimized views. One projection might maintain a SQL table for dashboard queries. Another might build a search index. A third might populate a cache. Each is independently optimized.
segments.thought_prompt: What consistency guarantee do projections provide? Are reads always up to date?

segments.text: The read side is eventually consistent with the write side. There's a small delay between writing an event and the projection updating. For most use cases this lag is acceptable. For critical reads, you can read directly from the event store.

Kafka is a natural fit for event sourcing. Its immutable, append-only log stores events durably. Consumer groups power projections. Retention policies keep the full history. And log compaction can maintain the latest state per entity as a bonus.

Event sourcing and CQRS add complexity, so they're not for every system. But for domains with complex business logic, audit requirements, or evolving read patterns, they're transformative. Think banking, e-commerce order processing, and real-time analytics pipelines.
